idiom_name: one opaque struct type per state + transition functions returning the next state's type
implementation_notes: C has no generics, so the state is encoded by giving each state its own opaque struct type (struct file_closed; struct file_open;) and letting only the functions that accept that type act on it; a transition returns a pointer to the next state's type, so obtaining the new handle is the only way to reach it. The compile-time check covers which operations are callable in a state, not the pattern's consume half: pointers are freely copyable, so aliases can outlive a transition and the state must be documented and nulled by convention. Where the protocol is decided at run time, the honest C answer is a state enum plus a transition table (the State pattern with function-pointer states, as in CFSM) rather than duplicated per-state APIs.
pitfalls: Pointers are copyable, so 'consumed by the transition' cannot be enforced: null out the caller's pointer and document single ownership, or the same state is reachable through several aliases.
Every state duplicates its declarations in the header; a protocol with more than a handful of states multiplies the API instead of simplifying it.
Passing handles through void * (callbacks, queues, plugin boundaries) erases the state distinction and re-opens exactly the runtime checks the encoding was meant to remove.
